tips.title: Use fans before air conditioning
tips.text: Fans use a fraction of the energy of air conditioning; often, moving air is all a room needs.

tips.title: Seal gaps around doors and windows
tips.text: Draughts let heated or cooled air escape; simple seals and door sweeps keep the air you paid to condition inside.

tips.title: Work with the sun
tips.text: Close curtains on sun-facing windows in the hot part of the day to keep rooms cooler; in cold weather, open them and let the sun warm the room.

tips.title: Switch to LED bulbs
tips.text: LEDs use far less energy than incandescent bulbs and last much longer, so each switch saves twice — power and replacements.

tips.title: Use daylight first
tips.text: Arrange work and reading near windows, and switch lights off in empty rooms; the cheapest light is the one already coming through the glass.

tips.title: Kill standby power
tips.text: Many devices draw power while switched "off". A switchable power strip turns a whole group off at once — chargers, TVs, and consoles included.

tips.title: Run full loads
tips.text: Washing machines and dishwashers use nearly the same energy partly loaded; full loads mean fewer cycles for the same work.

tips.title: Set the fridge right
tips.text: Keep the fridge near 4 °C and the freezer near −18 °C; colder settings waste energy without keeping food any safer. A fridge works best neither empty nor overpacked.

tips.title: Shorter, cooler showers
tips.text: Heating water takes real energy; shorter showers at a lower temperature cut water and energy use together.

tips.title: Consider rooftop solar
tips.text: Solar panels turn a roof into a small power station; even a small system can cover daytime basics like lights, fans, and charging. Start by checking how much sun your roof gets and how much power you use in the daytime.

tips.title: Take one small solar step
tips.text: If a full system is too big a step, solar garden lights, a solar power bank, or a solar water heater each cut one slice of grid use.
